partial_progress.details: Phase 6 of 11 complete and committed cleanly (depth-first, one phase closed before the next opened). Phase 6 enforced both previously-declared-but-unenforced timeout bounds: a new gate_registry_exec_bounded primitive runs each migrated gate under its registry timeout_s (process-GROUP kill, declare -p state-dump/reconcile protocol across the required subshell boundary), and run-all.sh gained a uniform RUN_ALL_SUITE_TIMEOUT_S (default 600s) applied identically in its sequential and parallel paths via `timeout -k 5`. Both bounds are proven to fire against deliberately-stalled synthetic fixtures; a full un-scoped verify-deploy.sh run on an idle machine converged to exactly Phase 5's documented failure set with zero new failures and zero bound trips. A real flake (an overly-broad process-name-matching leftover check) was caught and fixed during this phase's own verification. Pausing at this clean phase boundary rather than opening Phase 7 (gate-level concurrency scheduler) given the real-world time already spent on this dispatch (extensive design/testing of the subshell-based timeout mechanism, a full-battery idle measurement, and six existing regression suites plus two new test files re-run for confirmation).

memory_candidates.content: To add a killable, bounded timeout to a bash FUNCTION call (not an external command) while preserving its mutations to caller-scope globals: the function must run in a real forked subshell (required for interruptibility -- a same-process call can never be killed mid-flight), which strands any global mutation unless explicitly carried back. Fix: group the function call AND a `declare -p VAR1 VAR2...` dump of the exact variable names the caller cares about into ONE backgrounded job (`{ fn; declare -p ...; exit $rc; } &`), writing the dump to a file; the caller then `source`s that file after the job completes to restore continuity. Critically, the function call and the dump must be the SAME backgrounded job -- `fn & ...; wait; declare -p ...` one level up silently loses every mutation, because `&` always forks regardless of job-control mode, so a dump taken after a separate `wait` reads a different process's memory than the one that actually ran the function.

GNU coreutils `timeout`'s exit-status contract is bimodal, not a single sentinel: 124 when the initial SIGTERM was enough to end the command, and 137 (128+SIGKILL) when `-k SECS`'s escalation to SIGKILL was actually needed (the command ignored or blocked SIGTERM). A consumer that only checks `rc -eq 124` will silently miss detecting 'the bound fired' for any command that traps/ignores TERM -- both values must be checked wherever `timeout -k` is used and the caller wants to distinguish 'timed out' from 'failed on its own'.

A test asserting 'no leftover process remains after a kill' must capture and check the SPECIFIC child pid the test itself spawned (e.g. write the backgrounded job's own pid to a file, then check that EXACT pid's liveness afterward), never a broad command-line-pattern process search. Under any real concurrent test battery (a parallel suite runner, or simply a busy shared dev machine with sibling sessions), a pattern-based search can collide with an UNRELATED process that happens to share the same command text (e.g. two different test suites both using the same stalling command as a fixture), producing an intermittent false-positive failure that has nothing to do with the code under test.

Never hand-edit a large shared JSON state file (e.g. a multi-project task-tracker state.json) with a generic serializer like Python's `json.dump` using its DEFAULT `ensure_ascii=True` -- it re-escapes every non-ASCII character (em-dashes, smart quotes, any Unicode) across the ENTIRE file as `\uXXXX` sequences, producing a massive, misleading diff that touches every record even though no record's actual content changed. If a surgical field-level edit to such a file is genuinely needed, prefer a narrowly-scoped tool (e.g. `jq` with care for its own reformatting behavior, or a minimal in-place text substitution) over a full parse-mutate-dump roundtrip, and always diff the result before trusting it -- catching this immediately (before any commit) and reverting from a pre-edit backup is the correct recovery if it happens.
